questions.q: How does a Lakeflow job organise its tasks?

options.t: As a strict list run one after another, in the order they were added
options.why: Tasks form a DAG; independent tasks can run in parallel.

options.t: As a DAG of dependencies; independent tasks run in parallel
As separate jobs that must each be scheduled on their own
options.why: One job coordinates several tasks.

options.t: As notebooks that call each other with %run in sequence
options.why: Jobs define task dependencies, not notebook calls.

questions.explain: A job coordinates one or more tasks shown as a DAG; upstream tasks run first, in parallel where possible.

questions.q: A job must refresh a Lakeflow declarative pipeline before its SQL reporting step. Which task type runs the pipeline?

options.t: A notebook task that imports the pipeline's source files and executes them
options.why: Pipelines have their own pipeline task type.

options.t: A Run Job task pointing at the pipeline's name
options.why: Run Job calls another job; pipelines use the pipeline task.

options.t: A pipeline task
A SQL alert task that triggers the pipeline when data is stale
options.why: A SQL alert task evaluates an alert; the pipeline task runs a pipeline.

questions.explain: Task types include notebook, Python script, Python wheel, SQL, pipeline, ingestion pipeline, dashboard, Power BI, dbt, JAR, Spark Submit, Run Job, If/else, For each and SQL alert.

questions.q: One job should start another, already defined job as one of its steps. Which task type does that?

options.t: Run Job
For each, with the other job's name as the single input element
options.why: For each runs a nested task per element; Run Job calls another job.

options.t: If/else, with the other job as its true branch target
options.why: If/else branches inside a job; Run Job calls another job.

options.t: A notebook task that sleeps until the other job's schedule fires
options.why: Run Job starts another job directly.

questions.explain: The Run Job task type runs another job as a task.

questions.q: What is the default Run if condition of a task?

options.t: All done
options.why: The default is All succeeded.

options.t: At least one succeeded
options.why: The default is All succeeded.

options.t: None failed
options.why: The default is All succeeded.

options.t: All succeeded

questions.explain: Run if conditions: All succeeded (default), At least one succeeded, None failed, All done, At least one failed, All failed.

questions.q: A cleanup task must run after the main tasks whether they succeed or fail. Which Run if condition fits?

options.t: All succeeded, with retries on the main tasks so they always pass
options.why: All succeeded skips the cleanup when anything fails.

options.t: All done
At least one failed, so it runs only when something broke
options.why: That skips the cleanup on success.

options.t: None failed, which treats a failure as finished
options.why: None failed doesn't run when an upstream task failed.

questions.explain: All done runs the task regardless of upstream results, which is what cleanup needs.

questions.q: A task with Run if 'All succeeded' doesn't run because an upstream task failed. What status does it get?

options.t: Excluded
options.why: Excluded is for unmet failure-type conditions.

options.t: Skipped by concurrency
options.why: That concerns runs beyond maximum concurrent runs, not task conditions.

options.t: Upstream failed
Timed Out
options.why: Timed Out is for a task exceeding its timeout.

questions.explain: Unmet success-type conditions mark the task Upstream failed; unmet failure-type conditions mark it Excluded (skipped).

questions.q: A notification task has Run if 'At least one failed'. Every upstream task succeeds. What happens to the notification task?

options.t: It runs anyway, because conditions are checked only on failure
options.why: Its condition isn't met, so it doesn't run.

options.t: It is marked Upstream failed and fails the job
options.why: Unmet failure-type conditions mark the task Excluded.

options.t: It is marked Excluded (skipped)
It waits until an upstream task fails in a later run
options.why: It is evaluated per run and excluded in this one.

questions.explain: Unmet failure-type conditions (At least one failed, All failed) mark the task Excluded.

questions.q: Transformations should run only when the ingestion task actually added rows. Which task type implements that branch?

options.t: If/else condition
For each, iterating over the number of rows added by ingestion
options.why: For each loops; If/else branches on a boolean.

options.t: Run Job, pointing at a job that checks the row count first
options.why: If/else branches inside the same job.

options.t: A SQL alert task set to fail the job when no rows were added
options.why: If/else branches cleanly without failing the run.

questions.explain: An If/else condition task branches on a boolean expression, for example running transformations only if ingestion added rows.

questions.q: The same notebook must run once for each of 20 country codes. Which task type fits?

options.t: Twenty copies of the notebook task, one per country, edited by hand
options.why: For each runs one nested task per element.

options.t: If/else, with one branch per country code
options.why: If/else branches on a boolean; For each loops.

options.t: A Run Job task called twenty times from a notebook
options.why: For each is the looping task type.

options.t: For each

questions.explain: For each runs one nested task per element of an input array (a JSON array, task values or job parameters), with {{input}} available in the nested task.

questions.q: What is the default Concurrency of a For each task, and can it contain another For each?

options.t: Concurrency 10; nesting up to two levels is allowed
options.why: The default is 1, and a For each can't nest another For each.

options.t: Concurrency 1; it can't contain another For each
Unlimited concurrency; nesting is allowed
options.why: The default is 1, and nesting isn't allowed.

options.t: Concurrency equal to the cluster's cores; nesting is allowed
options.why: The default is 1, and nesting isn't allowed.

questions.explain: For each has a Concurrency setting (default 1); a For each can't nest another For each.

questions.q: Task `ingest` sets a task value named `rows`. How does a later task refer to it?

options.t: {{tasks.ingest.values.rows}}
{{job.parameters.ingest.rows}}, because task values become job parameters
options.why: Task values are referenced under tasks.<task>.values.

options.t: dbutils.widgets.get("ingest.rows") in the later notebook
options.why: The documented reference is {{tasks.<task_name>.values.<name>}}.

options.t: ${resources.tasks.ingest.rows}, the bundle substitution form
options.why: That is bundle syntax, not a task value reference.

questions.explain: A task sets a value with dbutils.jobs.taskValues.set(key = ..., value = ...); later tasks reference it as {{tasks.<task_name>.values.<task_value_name>}}.

options.t: dbutils.notebook.exit(value), which every later task can read
options.why: That returns a notebook result; task values use dbutils.jobs.taskValues.set.

options.t: spark.conf.set(key, value), which is shared across the job's tasks
options.why: Task values are set with dbutils.jobs.taskValues.set.

options.t: dbutils.jobs.taskValues.set(key = ..., value = ...)
By writing the value into the job's JSON definition at run time
options.why: Task values are set with dbutils.jobs.taskValues.set.

questions.explain: A task sets a task value with dbutils.jobs.taskValues.set(key = ..., value = ...).

questions.q: A job parameter `run_date` is defined at job level. Which tasks receive it?

options.t: Only the first task in the DAG
options.why: Job parameters are pushed to the job's tasks.

options.t: Only tasks that declare it in their own settings
options.why: Job parameters are pushed to tasks.

options.t: Only notebook tasks; SQL tasks can't receive parameters
options.why: Parameters are pushed to the job's tasks.

options.t: The job's tasks: job parameters are pushed down to them

questions.explain: A job has a trigger, parameters pushed to its tasks, notifications and Git settings.

questions.q: A task calls a flaky external API. How should its retries be configured?

options.t: Rely on the default, which always retries every task three times
options.why: The documentation is inconsistent about the default; set a retry policy explicitly.

options.t: Set a retry policy on the task, with a count and an interval
Wrap the whole job in a For each that repeats it until it works
options.why: Retries are set per task with a retry policy.

options.t: Use Run if 'All failed' on a copy of the task
options.why: A retry policy is the documented mechanism.

questions.explain: Add a retry policy per task (count and interval). The Databricks pages disagree on the default, so set it explicitly.

questions.q: A run shows the status 'Timed Out' for one task. What caused it?

options.t: The task ran longer than its Timeout setting
The task exceeded its duration warning threshold
options.why: A warning only raises an event for a notification; the timeout stops the task.

options.t: The cluster's auto-termination fired during the task
options.why: Timed Out comes from the task's own timeout.

options.t: An upstream task failed and the task was skipped
options.why: That would be Upstream failed.

questions.explain: A task's Timeout sets its maximum run time; exceeding it gives the status Timed Out. The Warning duration only raises an event.

questions.q: A task has a 30-minute timeout and two retries. How does the timeout apply?

options.t: To all attempts together: 30 minutes in total
options.why: The timeout applies to each retry.

options.t: Only to the first attempt; retries have no timeout
options.why: The timeout applies to each retry.

options.t: To each attempt
Only to the last retry
options.why: The timeout applies to each retry.

questions.explain: With both a timeout and retries, the timeout applies to each retry.

questions.q: What does a task's duration warning do when it is exceeded?

options.t: Stops the task and marks it Timed Out
options.why: That is the timeout.

options.t: Retries the task once with more compute
options.why: A warning only raises an event.

options.t: Cancels the whole job run
options.why: A warning only raises an event.

options.t: Raises an event that can drive a notification

questions.explain: The Warning duration only raises an event (for a notification); the Timeout stops the task.

questions.q: Partner files land in a volume at unpredictable times, and processing should start soon after each drop. Which trigger fits?

options.t: A schedule every minute, checking whether anything arrived
options.why: A file arrival trigger starts the job when files land.

options.t: File arrival
Continuous, so a run is always active
options.why: File arrival starts runs only when files land.

options.t: Manual runs whenever someone notices new files
options.why: File arrival automates this.

questions.explain: A file arrival trigger starts the job when new files land in a Unity Catalog external location or volume; it fits unpredictable drops.

questions.q: How often does a file arrival trigger check for new files, and what does it cost?

options.t: About every minute, best effort, with no cost beyond the cloud's file listing
Every second, exactly, billed as an always-on cluster
options.why: It checks about every minute, best effort.

options.t: Every hour, using a dedicated serverless job each time
options.why: It checks about every minute with no extra cost beyond listing.

options.t: Only when someone opens the job page in the UI
options.why: It checks on its own about every minute.

questions.explain: File arrival checks about every minute, recursively and best effort, with no cost beyond the cloud's file listing; file events make it faster.

questions.q: A gold refresh should run whenever its silver source tables change, not on a clock. Which trigger fits?

options.t: Scheduled, every five minutes
options.why: That is time-based; a table update trigger is data-driven.

options.t: File arrival on the silver tables' storage folder
options.why: Table update watches tables, not files.

options.t: Table update
Model update
options.why: That watches models, not tables.

questions.explain: A table update trigger runs the job when source tables change; scheduled triggers are time-based.

questions.q: Which of these triggers are data-driven rather than time-based?

options.t: File arrival
Table update
Scheduled (cron)
options.why: A schedule is time-based.

options.t: A schedule paused in development mode
options.why: Still a time-based schedule.

options.t: Manual Run now
options.why: Manual runs aren't triggered by data.

questions.explain: Scheduled triggers are time-based; file arrival and table update triggers start runs when data changes.

questions.q: What does a Continuous job trigger do?

options.t: Runs the job every minute on a fixed schedule
options.why: A new run starts whenever one ends, not on a clock.

options.t: Starts a new run whenever the previous one ends
Runs the job once and never again
options.why: That is a manual run.

options.t: Runs each task in parallel with no dependencies
options.why: The trigger concerns runs, not task order.

questions.explain: With the Continuous trigger, a new run starts whenever one ends; Databricks recommends it for streaming jobs, where it also retries failed runs with exponential backoff.

questions.q: An hourly job's run takes 90 minutes, and maximum concurrent runs is at its default. What happens to the next hour's run?

options.t: It is queued and starts when the current run finishes
options.why: Runs beyond maximum concurrent runs are skipped.

options.t: It is skipped
It cancels the current run and starts fresh
options.why: Runs beyond the limit are skipped.

options.t: It runs in parallel on a second cluster
options.why: By default one run of a job runs at a time.

questions.explain: By default one run of a job runs at a time; runs beyond maximum concurrent runs are skipped.

questions.q: A workspace hits `429 Too Many Requests` when starting job tasks. Which documented limit has it reached?

options.t: 1,000 tasks in one job
options.why: That limit is per job definition; 429 relates to concurrent task runs.

options.t: 12,000 saved jobs
options.why: That limits saved jobs, not concurrent runs.

options.t: 10,000 job creations per hour
options.why: That limits job creation; 429 here relates to concurrent task runs.

options.t: 2,000 concurrent task runs per workspace

questions.explain: Limits: 2,000 concurrent task runs per workspace (429 Too Many Requests beyond), 10,000 job creations per hour, 12,000 saved jobs, 1,000 tasks per job.
